hint.markers: Puts a coloured dot on every planet, so you can find it even when it is far too small to see.
hint.markers@simple: Puts a coloured dot on each planet, so you can find it even when it is tiny.
hint.markers@advanced: Marks every body with a dot of fixed size on screen: at true scale, the planets themselves are smaller than a pixel.
hint.orbitNames: Writes each planet’s name on its orbit line, so you can tell which path is which.
hint.orbitNames@simple: Writes the planet’s name on its path.

hint.smallBodies: Shows Pluto and the other dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and the two belts. Off by default so the planets stay easy to read.
hint.smallBodies@simple: Shows Pluto, comets and the asteroid belt.
hint.smallBodies@advanced: Adds the dwarf planets, named asteroids, comets with their tails, and the asteroid and Kuiper belts as fields of dots (each dot stands for many real bodies).
hint.alwaysLit: Lights every body from where you look, so the night side is not black. Good for seeing surfaces; hides the day and night lesson.
hint.alwaysLit@simple: Lights every planet from your side, so nothing is dark. But then you cannot see day and night!
hint.alwaysLit@advanced: Lights each body from the viewpoint instead of the Sun: no night sides, phases or eclipse shadows. Good for surface detail, wrong for the geometry of sunlight.

scale.label: Scale

summary.trueScale: Real sizes, real distances. Space is almost entirely empty.
summary.trueScale@simple: Everything is as big and as far apart as in real life. Space is mostly empty!
summary.trueScale@advanced: True to scale: sizes and distances share one ruler. The planets fill almost none of the space between them.
summary.textbook: Like a textbook picture: real sizes, but the planets are pulled close together. Not to scale!
summary.textbook@simple: Like a picture in a school book: the planets are pulled close together. It is not really like this!
summary.textbook@advanced: Sizes true to each other, distances compressed: the picture most diagrams show. Not to scale.
summary.bigPlanets: Real distances, but the planets are drawn far too big – and they are still lost in empty space.
summary.bigPlanets@simple: The planets are made much bigger, but they are as far apart as in real life. They still look tiny!
summary.bigPlanets@advanced: Distances true, sizes exaggerated: even enlarged tenfold, the planets are specks along their orbits.
summary.everythingVisible: Made to show everything at once: the planets are drawn too big and too close together. Not to scale!
summary.everythingVisible@simple: The planets are made bigger and pulled closer, so you can see them all. It is not really like this!
summary.everythingVisible@advanced: Sizes exaggerated and distances compressed, so every body is visible at once. Not to scale.

birthday.title: Your birthday in space
birthday.intro: Pick the day you were born. You will see how old you are on every planet, where the planets stood that day and how far you have travelled.
birthday.intro@simple: When were you born? Pick the day and find out how old you are on the other planets!
birthday.intro@advanced: Pick a date of birth. Ages, days and weights are computed from each world’s orbital period, rotation and surface gravity.
birthday.calendarHint: First the year, then the month, then the day.
birthday.privacy: Nothing is saved or sent anywhere. Your birthday stays on this screen and is forgotten when you close the page.

birthday.privacyLink: While a birthday is entered, links to this page leave out the date.

birthday.distance@simple: Since you were born, you have travelled {distance} kilometres around the Sun – without ever leaving the ground! That is as far as {trips, plural, one {# trip} other {# trips}} to the Moon and back.
birthday.distance@advanced: Since your birth, Earth’s orbital motion has carried you {distance} km around the Sun at a mean {speed, number} km/s: {trips, plural, one {# return trip} other {# return trips}} to the Moon.

years.intro: A year is one trip around the Sun. Your birthday on another planet comes when it is back where it was on the day you were born.
years.intro@simple: A year is one trip around the Sun. Planets far away take much longer, so you are younger there!
years.intro@advanced: A year is the sidereal orbital period: your birthday on a planet is when it returns to the point of its orbit where it was at your birth.

days.intro: A day lasts from one sunrise to the next. On Mercury a day is longer than a year, so you have had more birthdays there than sunrises!
days.intro@simple: A day lasts from one sunrise to the next. On some planets the Sun rises again after a few hours, on others only after months!
days.intro@advanced: A solar day (sunrise to sunrise) follows from the sidereal rotation and the orbit: 1/solar = 1/sidereal − 1/year. Venus spins backwards, so its Sun rises every 117 Earth days.

sound.honest: Space is silent: sound cannot travel through empty space. These recordings are real measurements of radio and plasma waves, turned into sound.
sound.honest@simple: In space there is no air, so there is no sound. Space probes measured invisible waves, and scientists turned them into sounds we can hear.
sound.honest@advanced: Sound needs a medium, and the near-vacuum of space carries no audible pressure waves. These are antenna measurements of radio and plasma waves (electric fields), played through a speaker, some shifted down in frequency.
sound.shortcut: Sound on or off (always off when the app opens)

sunRadioBursts.title: Radio bursts from the Sun
sunRadioBursts.what: Not sound: radio waves from a giant solar flare on 28 October 2003, caught by the Cassini probe and shifted down so we can hear them. The falling whistle is a burst of electrons racing away from the Sun.
sunRadioBursts.what@simple: In 2003 the Sun had a huge explosion. The Cassini space probe caught its radio waves, and scientists turned them into sound. The falling whistle is the burst rushing away from the Sun.
sunRadioBursts.what@advanced: Type III radio bursts from the X17 flare of 28 October 2003, recorded by Cassini's Radio and Plasma Wave Science instrument 8.7 AU from the Sun. Flare electrons excite plasma oscillations whose frequency falls as they reach thinner plasma farther out; the recording is shifted down into the audible range.

earthChorus.title: Earth's dawn chorus
earthChorus.what: Not sound: radio waves in the radiation belts around Earth, measured with an antenna by the Injun 3 satellite. They happen to vibrate at frequencies we can hear, and they chirp like birds at dawn, hence the name.
earthChorus.what@simple: Around Earth there are invisible waves made by tiny, fast particles. A satellite measured them with an antenna, and we can play them as sound. They chirp like birds in the morning!
earthChorus.what@advanced: Whistler-mode chorus in the Van Allen belts: rising tones generated by electrons spiralling along Earth's magnetic field, recorded by Injun 3. The waves lie in the audio band, so the antenna's electric-field signal is played back unchanged: an electromagnetic wave, not a pressure wave.

jupiterWhistlers.title: Lightning on Jupiter
jupiterWhistlers.what: Not sound: radio waves from lightning, caught by Voyager 1's antenna in 1979 and played through a speaker. They whistle downwards because they were stretched out travelling along Jupiter's magnetic field. They were the first sign of thunderstorms on Jupiter.
jupiterWhistlers.what@simple: When Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter, its antenna caught radio waves from lightning. Played as sound, they whistle. That is how we first found out that Jupiter has thunderstorms!
jupiterWhistlers.what@advanced: Jovian whistlers recorded by Voyager 1's plasma wave instrument in 1979: lightning impulses disperse along closed magnetic field lines, the higher frequencies arriving first, hence the falling tone. The first (indirect) evidence of lightning on Jupiter.

saturnRadio.title: Saturn's radio voice
saturnRadio.what: Not sound: radio waves from Saturn's northern and southern lights, recorded by Cassini in 2003. They are far too high to hear, so they were shifted down 44 times and sped up: these 30 seconds are about 11 minutes at Saturn.
saturnRadio.what@simple: Saturn has northern lights, and they send out radio waves. The Cassini probe caught them. Scientists made them lower and faster so we can hear them. They sound spooky!
saturnRadio.what@advanced: Saturn kilometric radiation, the auroral radio emission, recorded by Cassini's RPWS on approach in 2003. Frequencies divided by 44, time compressed 22 times (30 s here ≈ 11 min). The rising and falling tones trace small radio sources moving along auroral field lines.

teasers.sunEarth: Our whole world is a dot beside its star: 109 Earths fit across the Sun.
teasers.sunEarth@advanced: The Sun is 109 Earth diameters across and holds 333,000 times Earth’s mass.
teasers.sunEarth@simple: Next to the Sun, our big Earth is just a tiny dot.
teasers.sunPlanets: The Sun holds 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system.
teasers.sunPlanets@advanced: The Sun holds 99.86% of the solar system’s mass; Jupiter has most of what is left.
teasers.sunPlanets@simple: The Sun is heavier than all the planets together, about 750 times over.
teasers.jupiterAcrossSun: About ten Jupiters fit across the Sun, and eleven Earths across Jupiter.
teasers.jupiterAcrossSun@advanced: Each step is a factor of ten: the Sun is 10 Jupiter diameters, Jupiter 11 Earth diameters.
teasers.jupiterAcrossSun@simple: Line up ten Jupiters to cross the Sun, and eleven Earths to cross Jupiter.
teasers.planets: Jupiter is more than twice as heavy as all the other planets put together.
teasers.planets@advanced: Jupiter has 2.5 times the combined mass of the other seven planets.
teasers.planets@simple: Jupiter is heavier than all the other planets together, twice over.
teasers.marsSmall: Earth is twice as wide as Mars, and Mars only twice as wide as our Moon.
teasers.marsSmall@advanced: Mars has 53% of Earth’s diameter but only 11% of its mass.
teasers.marsSmall@simple: Mars is only about half as wide as Earth, much smaller than most people think.
teasers.iceGiants: Near-twins, each about four Earths wide, yet the smaller one, Neptune, is the heavier.
teasers.iceGiants@advanced: Their diameters differ by 3%, about four Earths each; denser Neptune has 18% more mass.
teasers.iceGiants@simple: Two blue twins, each about four Earths wide. Neptune is a bit smaller, but heavier.
teasers.earthMoon: The Moon is about a quarter as wide as Earth, and 30 Earths would fit in the gap between them.
teasers.earthMoon@advanced: The Moon has 27% of Earth’s diameter; on average they are 30 Earth diameters (384,400 km) apart.
teasers.earthMoon@simple: Thirty Earths in a row would just about reach the Moon.
teasers.bigForItsPlanet: Ganymede is bigger than our Moon, yet beside Jupiter it is a speck. For its planet, our Moon is the biggest of all.
teasers.bigForItsPlanet@advanced: The Moon has 27% of Earth’s diameter, Ganymede under 4% of Jupiter’s: no other planet has so large a moon for its size.
teasers.bigForItsPlanet@simple: Next to its planet, our Moon is huge. Ganymede is bigger, but next to Jupiter it looks tiny.
teasers.bigMoons: Our Moon comes only fifth, and every one of these is bigger than Pluto.
teasers.bigMoons@advanced: Ganymede and Titan outsize Mercury, our Moon ranks fifth, and all seven are larger than Pluto.
teasers.bigMoons@simple: Our Moon is only the fifth biggest. Four of these seven go around Jupiter.
teasers.galileanMoons: Galileo saw them circle Jupiter in 1610: proof that not everything goes around the Earth.
teasers.galileanMoons@advanced: Found by Galileo in 1610; Io, Europa and Ganymede orbit in step, 4 : 2 : 1.
teasers.galileanMoons@simple: In 1610 Galileo saw these moons going around Jupiter. So not everything goes around the Earth!
teasers.potatoMoons: Mars’s two moons are lumpy rocks the size of a city: Phobos is only 22 km across.
teasers.potatoMoons@advanced: Phobos (about 22 km) and Deimos (about 12 km) are too small for gravity to pull them round; they may be captured asteroids.
teasers.potatoMoons@simple: Mars has two tiny, lumpy moons shaped like potatoes. The bigger one would fit inside a city.
teasers.earthTwin: Almost the same size as Earth, but hot enough to melt lead, and one turn takes longer than its year.
teasers.earthTwin@advanced: 95% of Earth’s diameter, but 465 °C under 90 bar of carbon dioxide; it turns backwards, once in 243 days.
teasers.earthTwin@simple: Venus is almost as big as Earth, but hotter than an oven. It spins so slowly that one turn takes longer than a year.
teasers.moonsBeatPlanet: Ganymede and Titan are wider than the planet Mercury, yet Mercury is more than twice as heavy.
teasers.moonsBeatPlanet@advanced: Ganymede (5,268 km) and Titan (5,150 km) exceed Mercury (4,879 km), but Mercury’s iron core gives it over twice their mass.
teasers.moonsBeatPlanet@simple: Two moons are bigger than a planet! But Mercury is made of heavier stuff, so it is heavier.
teasers.weighMost: On the Moon you would weigh a sixth of what you weigh at home; at Jupiter’s cloud tops, two and a half times as much.
teasers.weighMost@advanced: Surface gravity: Moon 0.17 g, Mars 0.38 g, Earth 1 g, Jupiter 2.5 g at the cloud tops.
teasers.weighMost@simple: On the Moon you would be very light. On Jupiter you would be more than twice as heavy as at home.
teasers.plutoMoon: Pluto is only two thirds as wide as our Moon, and the Moon is more than five times as heavy.
teasers.plutoMoon@simple: Pluto is smaller than our Moon! Our Moon is much heavier too.
teasers.plutoMoon@advanced: Pluto has 68% of the Moon’s diameter and only 18% of its mass: one reason it is a dwarf planet.

about.text: Orbitalia is a free app for exploring the solar system: how big space really is, and how everything in it moves. It is made for classrooms, and for anyone who loves to look up.

feedback.title: Send feedback
feedback.lead: Found something wrong, have an idea, or want to say something? Orbitalia is free and open source, and it gets better with what you tell us. We read every message.
feedback.lead@simple: Is something broken? Do you have an idea? Write to us. We read every message!

message.label: Your message
